newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM, Okinawa disagree over U.S. base leases.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM, Okinawa disagree over U.S. base leases.

text.p: Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Tuesday failed to win crucial support from the governor of Okinawa to resolve the thorny issue of leases on land for U.S. military bases.
Hashimoto's talks with Governor Masahide Ota followed the prime minister's agreement with visiting U.S. Vice President Al Gore on Monday not to reduce the size of U.S. forces in Japan and east Asia.
Hashimoto is seeking to settle differences with Okinawa before May 14, when the central government's leases on privately owned land used by U.S. forces expire.
The land, owned by some 3,000 Okinawans who refuse to renew the leases, covers 362,000 sq metres (433,000 sq yards) on 12 bases including the U.S. Air Force's huge Kadena Air Base.

With the clock ticking, Hashimoto sought but failed to get Ota's support for his plan to push through parliament special measures to allow the government to continue providing the land to U.S. forces.

"We cannot agree to the revision of the law," Ota told reporters after his two-hour meeting with Hashimoto. "We cannot support the revision of the special land lease law given the hard feelings of the Okinawan people."

Hashimoto must now balance his commitment to Washington against the sentiments of Okinawa and the view of the small parties whose support gives his Liberal Democratic Party a working majority in parliament.
The parties, the Social Democrats and Sakigake Party, have said they oppose the emergency lease law revision and have called for Japan-U.S. discussions on troop cuts.
Okinawa houses more than 75 percent of all U.S. military facilities in Japan, a legacy of the 27-year U.S. occupation which followed a bloody World War Two battle there in 1945.
Local authorities on Okinawa, where about half of the 40,000 U.S. troops in Japan are stationed, want the bases closed by 2015, an action Tokyo strongly opposes.
A public outcry against the huge U.S. military presence there flared up in September 1995 after the rape of a local schoolgirl by three U.S. servicemen.
Japan and the United States last year agreed on a plan to streamline U.S. bases on Okinawa but without cutting the 28,000 U.S. military personnel stationed there.
